evidence.finding: Service level reached a minimum of 75%, but averaged 85.98% from incident start onward versus 87.66% before the incident; the post-incident average remained above the 80% target.
Mean offered calls increased 5.45% after the incident boundary, from 76.29 to 80.44 calls per interval.
Mean ASA increased 12.29%, from 29.42 to 33.03 seconds, indicating some transient customer-delay impact.
No operational events were visible in the evaluation window.
Handle time did not increase: mean AHT decreased 1.35%, from 377.26 to 372.15 seconds.

primary_root_cause_detail: A brief interval-level service-level breach occurred, but window-level performance remained above target and the visible data do not yet establish a sustained operational incident.
recommended_actions: Continue interval-level monitoring and alert only if service level remains below 80% for multiple consecutive intervals or the rolling-window result falls below target.
Review queue-level and staffing diagnostics before assigning an operational root cause if the breach recurs.
Retain the moderate volume increase as context, but do not classify it as a demand spike without a larger or sustained forecast variance.

rejected_hypotheses.reason: Post-incident mean AHT decreased rather than increased.
No platform or other operational event was visible.
Offered volume rose only 5.45% on average, which supports moderate pressure rather than a clear demand spike.

stakeholder_summary: CC-014 appears to be a brief, unsustained service-level variance rather than a material incident. Service level dipped to 75% in at least one interval, but averaged 85.98% after 09:45 and there were no visible events; moderate volume growth and higher ASA may have added temporary pressure.
